title: Key lookup and bookmark lookup
description: Identify key lookups in execution plans and learn how to eliminate them with covering indexes or index redesign.

data.text: A key lookup occurs when SQL Server uses a nonclustered index to find matching rows but then must retrieve additional columns from the clustered index or heap. For each row found in the nonclustered index, a separate lookup is performed, which adds random I/O and CPU overhead.

In an execution plan, a key lookup appears as the Key Lookup operator for clustered indexes, or the RID Lookup operator for heaps. These operators are usually placed to the right of an Index Seek or Index Scan and feed into the parent operator.

data.title: Query that triggers a key lookup
data.content: This query filters on OrderDate but selects CustomerName and TotalAmount, which are not in the index.

data.title: Fixing the key lookup with a covering index
data.content: Adding the missing columns to the index as included columns removes the need for lookups.

data.title: Many lookups are expensive
data.text: A single key lookup is cheap, but thousands or millions of them are not. If the execution plan shows a Key Lookup with a high row count, treat it as a performance problem and consider a covering index.

data.title: Ways to remove key lookups
items: Add the missing columns to the index using INCLUDE
Redesign the index so the key columns already cover the query
Use a columnstore index for analytical queries that need many columns
Rewrite the query to select only the columns in the existing index

data.title: Takeaway
points: Key lookups happen when a nonclustered index lacks needed columns
They appear as Key Lookup or RID Lookup operators in plans
Covering indexes eliminate lookups by storing all needed columns
Always evaluate whether the cost of the lookup outweighs the cost of a wider index
data.takeaway: Key lookups are the single most common sign that an index is almost right but not quite complete.
